title: Claude Code Dynamic Workflows OSS Expansion and CSM Skill Suite Research Finding

tldr.content: The prior research conclusion holds and is strengthened by OSS evidence: use a shared bounded worker runtime beneath csm-orchestrate, not separate schedulers in every skill. The closest script-level analogues are pi-dynamic-workflows, pi-subagents, open-dynamic-workflows, and cc-fleet; LangGraph, Microsoft Agent Framework, and Temporal supply complementary orchestration or durability primitives. Extend this repo first with worker/task contracts, revisioned graph patches, leases, event history, snapshots, adapters, and a live renderer while preserving skill-specific acceptance authority.

executiveSummary.content:
This DEEP hybrid expansion reuses the prior Claude Code finding, then adds five new research tracks covering OSS workflow runtimes, general agent frameworks, observability systems, local CSM extension seams, and a second pass over official Claude behavior. The OSS evidence is mostly project-authored README/source/CI evidence, so it demonstrates implementation shape and engineering intent, not independent production reliability.

```text
Claude Code reference
  generated JS harness -> bounded workers -> results/barriers -> workflow viewer

OSS lessons
  script runtime | graph runtime | durable workflow | coding-agent harness | OTel viewer
       |                 |             |                  |                /
        +----------------+-------------+------------------+---------------+
                                      v
                         CSM shared worker runtime
                 policy -> task graph -> leased attempts
                 events -> snapshots -> CLI/dashboard views
                 gates/receipts remain acceptance authority
```

The main architectural insight is compositional. A dynamic workflow needs a planner or model to propose work, a runtime to validate and schedule it, workers to execute within explicit boundaries, durable state to survive replay, and a separate observability projection. No reviewed OSS project provides Claude Code feature parity. The recommended repository evolution is therefore a narrow, provider-neutral runtime contract that lets existing skills opt into bounded fan-out and dynamic overlays without surrendering their current state machines, ledgers, artifact lineage, or human approval boundaries.

keyFindings.content:
K1 [supported] Claude Code dynamic workflows move loops, branching, fan-out, and intermediate results into a JavaScript runtime; `agent()`, `pipeline()`, `parallel()`, and `args` are documented primitives, while the workflow script has no direct filesystem/shell access and cannot import modules. [ref-claude-workflows][ref-claude-article]

K2 [supported] The workflow viewer reports phases, agent counts, tokens, elapsed time, recent agent prompts/tool calls/results, and controls for pause, stop, restart, and resume. It is a product UI, not a documented stable public progress API, and it does not establish exact completion percentage or ETA. [ref-claude-workflow-watch][ref-claude-workflow-limits]

K3 [partially-supported] `pi-dynamic-workflows`, `pi-subagents`, `open-dynamic-workflows`, and `cc-fleet` are the closest reviewed OSS analogues because their project documentation and source expose Claude-like script primitives, parallel fan-out, bounded workers, persistence/replay, and progress/viewer surfaces. This is an analogue classification, not proof of feature equivalence or production readiness. [ref-pi-dynamic][ref-pi-subagents][ref-open-dynamic][ref-cc-fleet]

K4 [partially-supported] `pi-dynamic-workflows` and `pi-subagents` provide unusually detailed visible implementations for workflow execution, concurrency limits, worktrees, replay/persistence, and live UI. Their evidence remains project-authored; third-party adapter compatibility, security, and production reliability are unverified. [ref-pi-dynamic-source][ref-pi-subagents-source]

K5 [supported] `open-dynamic-workflows` has broad multi-CLI portability and dashboard claims plus visible runtime/store/live-view source, but its README and source describe resume/journaling maturity inconsistently. It should be studied, not adopted without pinning and executable verification. [ref-open-dynamic][ref-open-dynamic-source]

K6 [partially-supported] `cc-fleet` documents a detached workflow engine, content-hash journaling, per-leaf restart/resume, budgets, a TUI board, and race-enabled CI tests. Its dependence on Claude CLI/provider semantics means third-party behavioral parity remains unverified. [ref-cc-fleet][ref-cc-fleet-source]

K7 [supported with qualification] `oh-my-claudecode` is a large active Claude Code skill/hook/team ecosystem, but it is not established as a portable JavaScript workflow runtime. `overstory` offers hierarchical workers, worktrees, SQLite mail, dashboards, tracing, and replay, but its repository is archived and says it is no longer maintained. [ref-omc][ref-overstory]

K8 [partially-supported] LangGraph supplies strong general-purpose primitives for dynamic fan-out/routing, checkpointing, interrupts, streaming, and time travel, but it is an orchestration substrate rather than a Claude Code coding harness. Microsoft Agent Framework's Harness Agent is a close conceptual harness analogue with planning, compaction, files, shell, approvals, background agents, and telemetry, but samples and some capabilities are preview/experimental. [ref-langgraph][ref-langgraph-stream][ref-maf-harness][ref-maf-workflows]

K9 [supported with qualification] CrewAI provides OSS Python role/task Crews and event-driven Flows with persistence and human feedback; commercial AMP observability must be separated from OSS core. AutoGen offers dynamic speaker selection and experimental GraphFlow but is now maintenance mode. Temporal provides durable event-history replay, signals, updates, and activities, but dynamic handlers are a fallback and Temporal is not an agent or coding harness. [ref-crewai][ref-autogen][ref-temporal]

K10 [partially-supported] OpenTelemetry, Phoenix, Langfuse, AgentOps, and Helicone can visualize or record agent/request activity, but traces and streams do not independently prove task correctness or acceptance. Phoenix is a credible open, self-hostable Claude Agent SDK/Claude Code-adjacent dashboard route; “best” is not established. [ref-otel-genai][ref-phoenix][ref-langfuse][ref-agentops][ref-helicone]

K11 [supported] The current local csm-orchestrate runtime compiles pre-existing approach phases, selects from a fixed capability manifest, executes route nodes in a serial loop, awaits terminal child results, and has no found wiring from its trace constructor to a live event callback or stream. [ref-prior-finding][ref-phase-compiler][ref-orchestrate-runtime][ref-orchestrate-trace]

K12 [partially-supported] Existing skills contain valuable adaptive-worker ingredients: csm-build has dependency-ready safe batches and ownership partitioning; csm-review has dimension/chunk decomposition and severity-scaled challenge; csm-deep-research has tiered panel sizing and role separation; csm-make-tests has gap-driven generation and ledgers; csm-autoresearch has population/stagnation/migration and evaluator-owned safety. Their shared worker scheduler, leases/heartbeats, and event/snapshot contracts are not first-class in the inspected surfaces. [ref-build-select][ref-review-scaling][ref-research-scaling][ref-tests-scaling][ref-autoresearch]

K13 [recommendation] Centralize worker scheduling, dynamic overlays, leases, replay, events, snapshots, and adapter boundaries beneath csm-orchestrate. Let skills declare policies and domain contracts, and retain skill-specific lifecycle/acceptance authority. This is an architectural inference. [ref-local-seams][ref-langgraph][ref-temporal]

K14 [recommendation] Extend the suite in waves: shared runtime first; then csm-build, csm-review, csm-deep-research, csm-make-tests, and csm-autoresearch as measurable pilots; keep csm-grill human-confirmation-only and csm-ddd evidence-only; keep planning artifacts immutable and attach runtime expansion overlays. This ordering is a proposed pilot sequence, not a proven optimum. [ref-local-seams][ref-plan][ref-grill][ref-ddd]

K15 [recommendation] Trustworthy visualization must separate durable state, transient activity, estimated progress, and verified evidence. Use stable identifiers, monotonic event ordering, heartbeat/staleness, attempt/replay state, privacy redaction, and explicit indeterminate/degraded states. [ref-otel-genai][ref-langgraph-stream][ref-phoenix][ref-local-progress]

detailSections.content:
### Claude Code behavior to reproduce

The prior finding established that Claude Code's dynamic workflow is a generated harness, not merely a larger subagent call. The second pass adds important limits: the workflow script cannot import modules or directly touch the filesystem/shell; agents perform tool work. Resume is session-local and replay is prefix-sensitive: unfinished work restarts, and later fan-out agents can rerun. Workflow progress is visible in a dedicated viewer, but its detailed progress state is not documented as a stable public API.

The product therefore separates several concerns:

```text
model-authored control intent
        -> script runtime
             -> task fan-out and barriers
             -> worker contexts and tool calls
             -> cached/intermediate results
        -> progress viewer and controls
        -> final report/result
```

The previous research also established that subagent context isolation is not a security boundary, that OTel is complementary to hooks, and that token totals or elapsed time are activity signals rather than verified completion. Those qualifications remain mandatory.

### OSS analogue assessment

| Candidate | What it contributes | Evidence posture | Main reason not to copy wholesale |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| pi-dynamic-workflows | JS workflow DSL, `agent`/`parallel`/`pipeline`/`phase`, limits, worktrees, run persistence, live task panel | Project source, tests, CI, README | Pi-specific host/runtime; young project; no independent reliability/security evidence |
| pi-subagents | Broad Pi integration, worker-thread runtime, nested workflows, JSONL journal, resume, steering, FleetView, RPC | Project source, tests, CI, README | Pre-1.0; third-party adapters outside project CI; replay limitations around resumed agents |
| open-dynamic-workflows | Cross-CLI adapters, worker-thread runtime, workspaces, run store, live dashboard and logs | Project source, tests, README | Early release and README/source maturity contradiction |
| cc-fleet | Detached engine, content-hash journal, leaf control, budgets, TUI, race-enabled CI | Project source, docs, CI, README | Provider semantics and merge behavior not equivalent to native Claude |
| oh-my-claudecode | Claude Code-native skills, hooks, teams, autopilot, HUD, persistence patterns | Project source, docs, metadata | Primarily a skill/team ecosystem rather than portable workflow runtime |
| overstory | Coordinator hierarchy, isolated worktrees, SQLite mail, checkpoints, replay/trace, dashboard | Project source, docs, CI, metadata | Archived and explicitly unmaintained |
| LangGraph | Dynamic `Send` fan-out, `Command` routing, checkpoints, interrupts, streams, time travel | Official docs/source | Application-defined nodes; no coding-agent UX or Claude permission model |
| Microsoft Agent Framework | Harness Agent, todos, compaction, files/shell, approvals, background agents, workflow checkpoints | Official docs/source | Rapidly evolving; sample UX and experimental components |
| Temporal | Durable event history, deterministic replay, activities, signals, updates | Official docs/source | Durability platform, not an LLM/coding harness; deterministic constraints |

The most useful lesson is not that one project wins. The candidates occupy different layers. Script-level analogues answer “how can a model-authored program fan out workers?” Graph frameworks answer “how can a runtime validate and stream a dynamic execution graph?” Temporal answers “how can long-lived side effects and external messages survive failure?” Coding-agent harnesses answer “how does a worker safely inspect and modify a repository?” CSM should use these distinctions rather than adopt a brand name as an architecture.

### What to borrow and what not to borrow

Borrow from the script runtimes:

- Runtime-created logical task keys rather than renumbering canonical plans.
- Bounded `parallel`/`pipeline` fan-out with explicit item limits.
- A barrier primitive before synthesis or aggregation.
- Per-leaf pause, stop, restart, and result inspection.
- A run store that can replay completed deterministic prefixes.
- A live task panel fed by structured runtime state.

Borrow from LangGraph:

- Dynamic fan-out represented as explicit sends/tasks.
- Typed stream modes for updates, messages, custom progress, checkpoints, and task lifecycle.
- Interrupts that are part of durable state rather than ad hoc prompts.
- Namespaces and run IDs that make nested work addressable.

Borrow from Temporal/Celery-style durability:

- Separate deterministic workflow control from worker side effects.
- Leases, acknowledgements, expiration, fencing, and at-least-once semantics.
- Event history and replay rules that are explicit rather than implied.
- External signals/updates for durable human or system input.

Borrow from observability systems:

- OTel-compatible trace/span correlation.
- Application-level task and acceptance events in addition to model/tool spans.
- Snapshot projection for fast UI reads.
- Redaction controls independent of operational metadata.

Do not borrow uncritically:

- README claims such as “production-ready,” “battle-tested,” “zero-trust,” “token savings,” or “semantic parity.”
- Hosted dashboards as proof of OSS-core behavior.
- A worktree fallback that silently executes in the shared tree.
- A trace closure or green UI row as proof that a skill's acceptance gate passed.
- Arbitrary model-generated graph mutation that can rewrite canonical plan or approach artifacts.
- A scheduler that treats task status as equivalent to artifact or evidence validity.

### Local extension boundary

The local implementation already has strong ingredients. csm-orchestrate's phase compiler validates canonical phase IDs, acyclic dependencies, capability manifests, effects, permissions, outputs, and idempotency. Its runtime requires an injected host and durable cursor store, validates child identity, retries based on effect/idempotency policy, reconciles artifacts, and runs technical/functional/final review gates. The gap is that route nodes are still precompiled and serial, and child invocation is terminal-result oriented.

The smallest shared vocabulary should be:

```text
WorkerPolicy
  role, model/tool adapter, permissions, effects, limits, retry, result schema, gates

TaskSpec
  logical task key, parent, graph revision, dependencies, input refs, policy ref

TaskAttempt
  attempt, worker id, lease/fence, status, timestamps, idempotency key, result ref

GraphPatch
  parent revision/digest, additions, dependencies, proposer, approval, new digest

RunEvent
  event id, sequence, run/phase/task/worker/attempt ids, time, status, redacted data

RunSnapshot
  current graph, tasks, workers, leases, activity, progress, gates, evidence, degradation
```

The graph patch is critical. Dynamic workers should add an immutable execution overlay or a new graph revision. They must never edit the original `csm-approach/1` or `csm-plan/1` artifact in place. A patch is accepted only when its parent digest matches, dependencies remain acyclic, capabilities and effects are allowed, ownership does not overlap, budgets remain available, and approval requirements pass.

### Skill-level mapping

**csm-orchestrate:** owns the shared runtime, graph revisions, scheduling, leases, event sink, snapshot materializer, host/model/tool adapters, and parent-level visualization. It remains responsible for route approvals and final receipt authority.

**csm-build:** first implementation pilot. Its existing ready-set and non-overlapping ownership rules naturally map to runtime tasks. Generated tasks should remain runtime overlay tasks, while canonical plan tasks remain stable. Integration and completion review stay build-owned.

**csm-review:** second pilot. Dimension-by-chunk is already a stable partition key. Finder/challenger input views must be enforced by the runtime so an adversarial worker cannot receive the author's rationale or an unreviewed scope. Severity determines challenge obligations, not just worker count.

**csm-deep-research:** third pilot. Tier-based panel sizing maps to a worker policy; evidence packets, citation checks, challenge isolation, judge scores, and verifier claims remain research-owned. A progress bar must not imply citation completeness.

**csm-make-tests:** fourth pilot. Generate workers can target modules, scenarios, mutation survivors, or performance surfaces. Artifact identity, approval, golden classification, mutation evidence, and ledger ownership remain make-tests-owned.

**csm-autoresearch:** strong specialized pilot. Candidate IDs, evaluator hashes, population islands, stagnation, migration, hard gates, and hash-chained ledgers already model dynamic work. The shared runtime should add leases/events/snapshots around candidate evaluations without replacing the experiment ledger. Its runtime correctly refuses unsupported network, memory, process, and descendant controls rather than claiming them.

**csm-plan:** keep canonical planning artifacts and task IDs stable. Planning may request or describe an execution overlay, but runtime-created work must not silently rewrite the saved plan or make pending implementation tasks appear complete.

**csm-grill:** do not add automatic worker dispatch. The one-question-at-a-time and explicit-confirmation boundary is the feature. It may emit user-approved hints about likely decomposition, but not execute them.

**csm-ddd:** keep deterministic, read-only evidence production. DDD graphs can suggest candidate partitions or seams, but hypotheses such as inferred or unverified must never become automatic execution authority.

### Progress and visualization

Use a two-level projection:

```text
Run snapshot
  -> overall weighted milestone bar
  -> phase/task tree
       -> worker rows: status, activity, heartbeat, attempt, model, cost
       -> evidence/gate rows: artifacts, validators, acceptance status
```

Required distinctions:

| Signal | Meaning | UI treatment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `running` | worker process/turn is active | animated activity indicator |
| `heartbeat age` | latest liveness signal | stale warning after policy threshold |
| `progress fraction` | skill-declared measurable milestone fraction | percentage only when declared/calculable |
| `activity summary` | bounded recent action/tool category | text summary, never correctness claim |
| `verified evidence` | artifact/gate/receipt support | separate acceptance indicator |
| `indeterminate` | no trustworthy estimate or lost event continuity | explicit unknown state |

The UI should display replayed, retried, cancelled, timed-out, blocked, and degraded-durability states rather than collapsing them into failed or completed. The event log is operational history; the snapshot is a read model; the terminal receipt and skill ledger remain authoritative. This mirrors the previous finding while incorporating LangGraph's custom/task streams and OTel's trace hierarchy without claiming either proves task success.

recommendation.content:
Recommend advancing the repository through a shared, opt-in dynamic execution layer:

1. Define versioned `worker-policy`, `task-spec`, `task-attempt`, `graph-patch`, `run-event`, `run-snapshot`, lease-store, event-store, model-adapter, and tool-adapter contracts under csm-orchestrate.
2. Implement a deterministic scheduler for static route nodes and runtime overlay tasks with bounded fan-out, dependency checks, capacity, timeout, cancellation, retry, idempotency, and fencing.
3. Emit append-only redacted events and materialize snapshots. Add CLI and HTML projections from snapshots, with an overall milestone view and worker detail view.
4. Add a model-directed decomposition boundary that accepts only typed task proposals. Validate graph revision, policy, capability, effect, budget, ownership, and approval before creating work.
5. Pilot csm-build, csm-review, csm-deep-research, csm-make-tests, and csm-autoresearch in that order only as a proposed sequence. Measure concurrency, replay, event loss, integration conflicts, and acceptance preservation.
6. Keep csm-plan's canonical tasks immutable, csm-grill's user confirmation boundary intact, and csm-ddd's evidence hypotheses non-authoritative.
7. Use Phoenix or another OTel-compatible OSS viewer as an optional external projection target, not as the source of truth. A repository-native snapshot renderer should remain available without a hosted dependency.
8. Require failure-mode tests before enabling dynamic mode: duplicate task proposal, concurrent graph patches, lease expiry, stale worker completion, worker restart, lost/out-of-order/duplicate events, redaction failure, provider mismatch, budget exhaustion, and partial barrier completion.
9. Do not claim Claude Code parity, productivity gains, or production readiness until controlled local evaluations demonstrate them.

The design should default to fixed mode. Dynamic mode earns activation only when task shape is genuinely unknown, parallelism materially helps, and the selected skill's policy can state measurable acceptance and safe replay semantics.

unverifiedClaims.content:
Decision-blocking: the repository still lacks a production `invokeSiblingSkill` host, worker scheduler, lease store, and event store. The research identifies interfaces and candidate patterns, not implementation feasibility.

Decision-blocking: Claude Code's internal workflow viewer, generated-script runtime, cache/replay implementation, and agent scheduling internals are proprietary; public documentation supports observed behavior but not internal parity.

Material risk: OSS repository evidence is primarily author-controlled README/source/CI evidence. Tests and CI show intended and locally exercised behavior, not independent production reliability or security.

Material risk: project status, star counts, licenses, provider support, and documentation change. Repository evidence should be pinned to commit/release before any adoption decision.

Material risk: open-dynamic-workflows has an observed README/source maturity inconsistency around resume/journaling. The exact behavior must be verified at a pinned commit.

Material risk: worktree isolation is not uniform. Some systems have fallbacks, some return diffs, some auto-commit branches, and some leave merge policy to the caller.

Material risk: context isolation, process isolation, filesystem isolation, credential isolation, network isolation, and evaluator isolation are separate properties. No reviewed analogue proves all of them together.

Material risk: replay, retry, lease expiry, and event delivery may produce duplicate side effects. Idempotency and fencing are design requirements inferred from durable execution semantics, not universal product guarantees.

Material risk: OTel traces, workflow viewers, token totals, elapsed time, and activity summaries do not prove task correctness or acceptance.

Informational: LangGraph, CrewAI, Microsoft Agent Framework, Temporal, Phoenix, AgentOps, Langfuse, and Helicone are complementary layers with different languages, licensing, maturity, and hosted/open-source boundaries.

Unverifiable: dynamic workers will improve this repository's productivity, cost, latency, autonomy, correctness, or user trust without repository-local controlled experiments.

references.content: References are encoded in the top-level `references` array. External project README/source/CI claims are labeled as author-controlled or inspected project evidence in the detail section; official Anthropic, framework, and observability documentation is distinguished from inference. All sources were retrieved or inspected on 2026-08-27.

processAppendix.content:
Triage: DEEP, hybrid. This expansion could change the architecture of the CSM suite and specifically requested OSS articles and repositories claiming Claude Code-like behavior.

Prior evidence consumed: the run-owned prior finding `2026-08-27-claude-code-dynamic-workflows-skills-20260827t120000z-d7e8f9a0b1c2-research.json` was read and its Claude Code findings, local architecture map, progress model, caveats, and recommended shared runtime were incorporated.

Research tracks: (1) six candidate Claude-like OSS workflow repositories; (2) LangGraph, CrewAI, Microsoft Agent Framework, AutoGen, and Temporal; (3) OpenTelemetry GenAI, Phoenix, AgentOps, Langfuse, and Helicone observability; (4) local CSM runtime and skill extension seams; (5) official Claude Code workflow, SDK, streaming, session, hook, and progress behavior. Five independent read-only researchers returned structured findings.

OSS comparison method: record project claims, inspect source/docs/CI where available, classify evidence as project-authored or directly inspectable, note license/activity/status, and explicitly separate analogue capability from feature parity, security, or production outcome. No candidate repository was cloned, executed, or modified.

Synthesis: found four close script-runtime analogues, two strong hierarchical/skill ecosystems, three complementary orchestration/durability frameworks, and five observability layers. Convergent design lessons were stable task keys, bounded concurrency, explicit replay, worktree policy, event streams, snapshots, and acceptance authority outside observability.

Challenge: the independent challenger downgraded claims that all four OSS projects implement every listed feature, removed unsupported superlatives such as strongest/closest/best, required separating README claims from source evidence, corrected the overstatement of Phoenix licensing/compatibility, and required status and pinning caveats.

Judge: factual accuracy 0.86, citation accuracy 0.78, completeness 0.84, clarity 0.91; PASS. Required final corrections were applied: dated/pinned evidence caveat, license/source-availability distinction, no undocumented-API absence claim, no production-reliability inference from tests, and explicit definitions of activity versus completion.

Verification: all fixed sections are present and ordered; claim citations resolve to references; journal sequences are contiguous; no declared artifacts exist; no credentials, tokens, private keys, or personal data are included. Current worktree baseline was an untracked prior research artifact; this new finding is the only intended additional persistent write. No commit was created because the user did not explicitly request a commit in this invocation.

citations.locator: repository README and graph API docs
citations.quote: A low-level stateful-agent orchestration layer can provide dynamic routing and persistence without replacing application-specific nodes.
Separating deterministic workflow control from external Activities supports replayable long-running execution.

claims.statement: The proposed pilot order is shared runtime, csm-build, csm-review, csm-deep-research, csm-make-tests, and csm-autoresearch, while csm-grill remains human-confirmation-only, csm-ddd remains evidence-only, and planning artifacts remain immutable with execution overlays.

citations.quote: Planning never authorizes implementation and future build consumes a saved plan; canonical planning tasks remain a separate execution contract.
Grill is an agreed approach with one-question-at-a-time user confirmation and never plans or implements.
DDD produces deterministic read-only report/graph evidence and treats inferred/unverified claims as hypotheses.
Build, review, research, make-tests, and autoresearch already expose measurable partitions or runtime-like state suitable for bounded pilots.

claims.statement: Worker visualization should distinguish durable state, transient activity, estimated progress, and verified evidence, with stable IDs, monotonic ordering, heartbeat/staleness, attempt/replay, redaction, and indeterminate/degraded states.

citations.quote: OTel provides correlation and operation lifecycle semantics, not application acceptance semantics.
Typed updates, messages, custom events, checkpoints, and task streams provide separate channels for runtime activity and state.

citations.locator: tracing and Claude Agent SDK integration
citations.quote: Trace visualization and hide_inputs/hide_outputs support observability with privacy controls, but not task acceptance.
Current local trace/cursor/journal fields provide correlation and coarse state but omit worker identity, leases, progress, and live subscription semantics.

claims.statement: Adopting dynamic workers or any reviewed OSS framework will improve repository productivity, cost, latency, autonomy, correctness, or user trust.

citations.locator: When and when not to use agents and Summary
citations.quote: Agentic systems trade latency and cost for performance; complexity should be added only when it demonstrably improves outcomes.
